title: Programming, DS & Algorithms
weightage: ~11-18 marks per paper (2024-2026 DA papers; roughly 4-6 one-mark + 4-6 two-mark questions incl. 3-5 Python code-tracing questions)
summary: High-yield, mostly tracing-based section: predict the output of Python snippets (recursion, closures, mutable defaults, list aliasing), simulate sorts/searches/traversals, and reason about simple complexity. Depth is modest but accuracy on code tracing decides the marks.
notesGuide: 1) Base course: NPTEL 'Programming, DS & Algorithms using Python' (nptel.ac.in/courses/106106145) - download the lecture slides/transcripts from the course page and keep one page of notes per week. 2) Download MIT 6.006 Spring 2020 lecture-note PDFs (OCW 'Lecture Notes' page) for sorting, hashing, BFS/DFS and Dijkstra, and Open Data Structures (ods-python.pdf) chapters 2-3 (array/linked structures), 5 (hashing), 6 (BSTs), 12 (graphs). 3) For Python, build a 'traps sheet' from the official docs: mutable default args (Tutorial 4.8.1), closures/scoping (Execution Model), list aliasing vs copy, slicing with negative steps, integer vs float division, dict/set ordering, string immutability - write each trap as a 3-line snippet + output. 4) Make a one-page 'algorithm card' table: for each search/sort - best/avg/worst time, space, stable?, in-place?, #swaps/#comparisons pattern, behaviour on sorted/reverse input. 5) Hand-trace every DA PYQ snippet on paper first, then confirm on pythontutor.com; log mistakes in an error notebook and revise it weekly.
